title: Endgames
description: Basic mates, king and pawn endings, and the two most important rook endgames.

steps.text: With king and queen against a lone king, use the queen to shrink the king's box, then walk your king over to help. In the final position the queen mates while your king guards the escape squares.
Deliver mate.
steps.hint: The queen can't be taken on g7 — your king protects it.

steps.text: One of these moves throws away the win. Which one?
steps.success: Right — after Qg6 Black has no legal move but isn't in check: stalemate, a draw.

lessons.title: Rook vs king
lessons.summary: Use your king and rook together.

steps.text: A rook alone can't mate — it needs its king. Push the enemy king to the edge, put your king opposite it, then check along the edge.
The kings face each other. Mate in one.

lessons.title: Mate with two bishops
lessons.summary: Side by side, the bishops build a wall.

steps.text: Two bishops can mate a lone king, but only in a corner. Keep the bishops next to each other so their diagonals form a wall, bring your king up, and squeeze the enemy king toward a corner. At the end your king covers the squares in front of the corner and the bishops do the rest.
Deliver mate.
steps.hint: The light bishop already covers g8. Check along the long diagonal.
steps.success: Checkmate: the king guards g7 and h7, one bishop covers g8, the other gives check.

lessons.title: Mate with bishop and knight
lessons.summary: The hardest basic mate: it needs the right corner.

steps.text: Bishop and knight can force mate, but only in a corner the bishop controls. This bishop moves on dark squares, so the enemy king must be driven to h8 or a1. If it runs to a light corner, push it along the edge to a dark one. The knight and king take away the last escape squares.
Finish it: mate in one.
steps.hint: The knight covers g8 and your king covers g7 and h7. Check along the long diagonal.
steps.success: Checkmate in the dark corner, exactly where the bishop rules.

lessons.title: The opposition
lessons.summary: The key idea of king and pawn endings.

steps.text: When the kings stand face to face with one square between them, the player who does NOT have to move has the opposition. The other king must step aside and give ground.
White to move. Who has the opposition?
steps.success: Correct — White must move, so Black holds the opposition and can stop the pawn.

lessons.title: Key squares
lessons.summary: Reach the right square and the pawn promotes.

steps.text: Every pawn has key squares: if your king reaches one, the pawn promotes no matter where the enemy king stands. For a pawn on the 2nd, 3rd or 4th rank they are the three squares two ranks in front of it. For this pawn on d4 that's c6, d6 and e6.
Now the pawn is on d2. Which squares are its key squares?
steps.success: Right, two ranks in front of the pawn. Get the king to c4, d4 or e4 and the pawn queens.

steps.text: White's king has reached d6, a key square of the d4 pawn. Black is to move. What happens?
steps.success: White wins. From a key square the king escorts the pawn home, whoever is to move.

lessons.title: Triangulation
lessons.summary: Lose a move with the king to put the opponent in zugzwang.

steps.text: With Black to move here, Black would have to give way and lose. With White to move, White would like to pass the move to Black. A king can't pass, but it can walk a triangle: d5-e5-d4-d5 takes three moves and returns to the same square. Black's king, short of room, can only step back and forth and can't keep pace.
Why a triangle of three moves, and not simply Kd4 and back to d5?
choices: Two moves there and back bring the same position back with the same side to move; three moves hand the move to Black
The king is safer on e5
steps.success: Right: an odd number of moves hands the move over. Black can't copy the triangle, so the same position returns with Black to move.

steps.text: The same position with Black to move is zugzwang: every move makes it worse. After ...Kc8, White's king steps to d6 and heads for c7; after ...Ke7, c5-c6! breaks through and a pawn queens.
Black to move. How does this end?
steps.success: Yes. With Black to move, every king move lets White in. That is exactly what the triangle achieved.

lessons.title: The square rule
lessons.summary: Can the king catch the pawn?

steps.text: Imagine a square from the pawn to its promotion rank (here b5–e5–e8–b8). If the defending king can step into that square, it catches the pawn. If not, the pawn queens.
Black to move. Can the black king catch the pawn?
steps.success: Yes — …Ke5 steps into the square and the king catches the pawn.

steps.text: Now the king is one file further away. Can it still catch the pawn?
steps.success: No — the king can't enter the square in time, and the pawn promotes.

lessons.title: The Lucena position
lessons.summary: Building a bridge to win a rook endgame.

steps.text: White's king is in front of its pawn on the seventh rank, and Black's king is cut off. White wins by "building a bridge": the rook goes to the fourth rank to shield the king from checks.
First push the black king further away with a check, then bring your rook to the fourth rank.
steps.hint: Check on the d-file, then Rd4.
steps.success: The bridge is ready: when the checks come, Rb4 will block them and the pawn queens.

lessons.title: The Philidor position
lessons.summary: How to draw a rook endgame a pawn down.

steps.text: The defender keeps the king in front of the pawn and the rook on its third rank (here the sixth), stopping the enemy king from advancing.
White has just pushed the pawn to e6. What is Black's drawing idea now?
choices: Check the white king from behind, from far away
Keep the rook on the sixth rank
Attack the pawn with the king
steps.success: Exactly — with the pawn on e6 the white king has no shelter, so endless checks from behind draw.

lessons.title: The wrong bishop
lessons.summary: Bishop and rook pawn: sometimes only a draw.

steps.text: An extra bishop and pawn usually win easily, but a rook pawn (a- or h-pawn) is special: the bishop must control the promotion square. h8 is a dark square and this bishop only ever stands on light squares, so it can never drive Black's king out of the corner.
Black to move. What is the result with best play?
steps.success: Draw. Black shuffles between h8 and g8, and White can't make progress without stalemating.

steps.text: Same position, but the bishop is on c1. Can White win now?
steps.success: Yes. A dark-squared bishop controls h8, so Black's king can be driven out and the pawn promotes.

lessons.title: Rooks behind passed pawns
lessons.summary: Tarrasch's rule, and why it works.

steps.text: Rooks belong behind passed pawns, your own or your opponent's. Behind its own pawn, the rook gains a square of range with every step the pawn takes and guards it all the way to promotion. In front of the pawn, the rook just gets in the way.
White wants to push the a-pawn. Where does the rook belong?
choices: a8, in front of the pawn
steps.success: Behind the pawn: from a1 the rook supports it on every square up to a8.

steps.text: Now Black has the passed a-pawn. Where should White's rook go to stop it?
choices: a1, in front of the pawn
steps.success: Behind it again: from a8 the rook attacks the pawn on every step, and the rook keeps more room the further the pawn goes.
